days.title: Add Decimals with Place Value
days.target: I can add decimals by aligning equal place values.
days.lecture: Line up decimal points so tenths are under tenths and hundredths under hundredths. Add zeros if helpful. Add from right to left, regroup, and bring the decimal point straight down.

examples.q: Use the standard algorithm: 85.9 + 2.9. Show your regrouping or division steps.
examples.steps: Align decimal points; 85.9 + 2.9 = 88.8.
worked_steps: Line up the decimal points. Add placeholder zeros so the numbers are 85.9 and 2.9.
Column 1 from the right: 9 + 9 = 18. Write 8 and carry 1 to the next column.
Column 2 from the right: 5 + 2 + 1 carried = 8. Write 8.
Column 3 from the right: 8 + 0 = 8. Write 8.
Bring the decimal point straight down, keeping 1 decimal place: 88.8. The simplified decimal answer is 88.8.

days.title: Multiply Decimals and Estimate
days.target: I can multiply decimals and use an estimate to place the decimal point.
days.lecture: Multiply as whole numbers using the standard algorithm. The product has the total number of decimal places in the two factors before trailing zeros are removed. Check its size against an estimate.

examples.q: Use the standard algorithm: 36.8 × 7.3. Show your regrouping or division steps.
examples.steps: Compute the whole-number product and restore decimal places: 36.8 × 7.3 = 268.64.
worked_steps: Estimate the size first. Treat the factors as whole numbers: 36.8 becomes 368, and 7.3 becomes 73.
Multiply the whole numbers: 368 × 73 = 26864.
Count decimal places: 1 in 36.8 plus 1 in 7.3 gives 2.
Place the decimal point 2 places from the right in 26864, adding leading zeros if necessary: 268.64. Remove only unnecessary trailing zeros.

days.title: Divide by a Decimal
days.target: I can divide by a decimal using an equivalent whole-number divisor.
days.lecture: Multiply both dividend and divisor by the same power of 10 so the divisor is a whole number. Then use long division, adding zeros to the dividend as needed. Check by multiplication.

examples.q: Use the standard algorithm: 46.8 ÷ 0.9. Show your regrouping or division steps.
examples.steps: Multiply both numbers by 10: 468 ÷ 9 = 52. Check: 0.9 × 52 = 46.8.
worked_steps: Make the divisor a whole number. Multiply BOTH numbers by 10: 46.8 ÷ 0.9 = 468 ÷ 9. This keeps the quotient unchanged.
9 goes into 46 5 times. Write 5; multiply 5 × 9 = 45; subtract 46 − 45 = 1.
Bring down the next digit, 8, to make 18. 9 goes into 18 2 times. Write 2; multiply 2 × 9 = 18; subtract 18 − 18 = 0.
Check using multiplication: 0.9 × 52 = 46.8. The quotient is 52.

days.unit_name: Positive Rational Numbers: Fractions and Mixed Numbers
days.title: Explain Fraction Models and Algorithms
days.target: I can explain Fraction Models and Algorithms, and explain and check my reasoning.
days.lecture: A quotient asks how many groups of the divisor fit in the dividend. Rename both fractions with a common denominator, draw equal parts, and count groups. A partial group is a fraction of the divisor, not of the original whole. If (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = q, then (c/d) × q = a/b. Multiplying by d/c undoes multiplying by c/d, so divide by a nonzero fraction by multiplying by its reciprocal. Simplify the product. Rename a mixed number as (whole × denominator + numerator)/denominator. Keep the dividend, change division to multiplication, and use the reciprocal of the divisor. Simplify and interpret the result. Identify the total amount and the size of one group. Use total ÷ group size for the number of groups. A quotient may include a partial group; if the question asks for full servings, use only the whole-number part.

days.lecture: Start at the origin. Move horizontally by x, then vertically by y. Quadrant signs are I (+,+), II (-,+), III (-,-), IV (+,-). A point on an axis belongs to no quadrant. Across the x-axis, keep x and reverse the sign of y. Across the y-axis, reverse x and keep y. Across both axes, reverse both signs. The reflected point stays the same distance from the axis. Plot both points. If x-coordinates match, count the vertical units; if y-coordinates match, count horizontal units. On opposite sides of zero, add distances to zero. On the same side, subtract magnitudes.

examples.steps: Move 7 right, then 2 down.

days.lecture: A statistical question anticipates different answers in a collection of data. Name the group, the measured attribute, and the expected variation. A question about one fixed fact is not statistical. Draw an equally spaced number line and stack one dot per observation above its value. Repeated values stack vertically. Add an axis label with units and check that the dot count equals the data count. The mean is a fair share: add all values and divide by the number of observations. Report the count and measurement units. A large unusual value can pull the mean toward it. A useful summary names the group and attribute, units, observation count, center, variability, and shape. days.title: Connect Rational Numbers, Expressions, and Ratios
days.target: I can connect Rational Numbers, Expressions, and Ratios, and explain and check my reasoning.
days.lecture: If (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = q, then (c/d) × q = a/b. Multiplying by d/c undoes multiplying by c/d, so divide by a nonzero fraction by multiplying by its reciprocal. Simplify the product. A number farther right is greater. Among negative numbers, the value closer to zero is greater. Use a common denominator or familiar benchmarks to compare negative fractions. Replace every variable with its assigned value, using parentheses. Apply the order of operations. In formulas, label the answer with the appropriate measurement units. Multiply both values in a ratio by the same scale factor. Organize pairs in a table and check that every row compares the same quantities in the same order.

examples.q: Calculate 1/2 ÷ 1/2. Simplify.
worked_steps: Rename the numbers as fractions: 1/2 = 1/2 and 1/2 = 1/2.
Keep the first fraction and multiply by the reciprocal of the second: 1/2 × 2.
Multiply numerators and denominators: (1 × 2) / (2 × 1) = 2/2.
Simplify by dividing top and bottom by 2: 1.
Check the result: 1/2 × 1 = 1/2, so the quotient is correct.

days.lecture: Define the unknown quantity. Translate the relationship into an equation before calculating. Use the inverse operation and check whether the answer makes sense in the situation. days.lecture: Plot both points. If x-coordinates match, count the vertical units; if y-coordinates match, count horizontal units. On opposite sides of zero, add distances to zero. On the same side, subtract magnitudes. Plot vertices in order and connect them, including the last to the first. Equal x-values make a vertical side; equal y-values make a horizontal side. Count or subtract coordinates to get the side lengths. A closed rectangular prism has two faces of area lw, two of lh, and two of wh. Add the six face areas: SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh. If a face is missing, do not include it. A rectangular prism has volume V = lwh = Bh, where B is base area. Fractional edge lengths still multiply. Use cubic units; surface area and volume measure different attributes.

problems.steps: Closed surface area = 2(8+20+10) = 76. Remove the top area 8: 68.

problems.q: A prism measures 5/2 m by 1 m by 5/2 m. Part A: enter its volume. Part B: how many cubes with edge 1/2 m fill it? Explain why the cube count differs from the cubic-meter volume.
problems.steps: Multiply edges: 5/2 × 1 × 5/2 = 25/4. The edge counts are 5, 2, 5, giving 50 cubes. Each cube is 1/8 m³; 50/8 = 25/4.

problems.q: Plot A(-7, -6), B(5, -6), and C(-7, 6). Part A: enter AB. Part B: enter AC and explain how zero helps find each distance.
problems.steps: AB is horizontal: 7 + 5 = 12. AC is vertical: 6 + 6 = 12. Each segment crosses an axis.

problems.q: Plot and connect (-3,-6), (3,-6), (3,3), (-3,3). Find the side lengths and area. Find the perimeter too.
problems.a: Sides 6 and 9; area 54 square units; perimeter 30 units
problems.steps: Horizontal length 3 - (-3) = 6; vertical length 3 - (-6) = 9; area = 6 × 9.

days.unit_name: AASA Applications and Cumulative Review
days.title: Explain Data and Critique Mathematical Claims
days.target: I can explain Data and Critique Mathematical Claims, and explain and check my reasoning.
days.lecture: A useful summary names the group and attribute, units, observation count, center, variability, and shape. Explain why the chosen center and spread fit the data and mention any striking value. Use operation properties to rewrite an expression. Matching values at one input do not prove equivalence for all inputs. A single counterexample is enough to show two expressions are not equivalent. Substitute each value and decide whether the comparison is true. A continuous number-line ray represents infinitely many real-number solutions. A real situation may restrict useful solutions to whole numbers. Find the mean. Calculate each value’s distance from the mean, add those distances, then divide by the number of observations. MAD describes a typical distance from the mean in the original units.

examples.q: Reading times in minutes are 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9. Write a summary with count, attribute, units, center, variability, shape, and a justified choice of measures.
examples.a: 6 observations of reading time in minutes. Mean 15/2 min, MAD 5/6 min; roughly symmetric, so mean/MAD are reasonable.
examples.steps: Calculate the center and spread before interpreting them in context. Other accurate, justified summaries are acceptable.
worked_steps: A useful summary names the group and attribute, units, observation count, center, variability, and shape.
Explain why the chosen center and spread fit the data and mention any striking value.
Calculate the center and spread before interpreting them in context.
Other accurate, justified summaries are acceptable.
State the result in the form requested: 6 observations of reading time in minutes. Mean 15/2 min, MAD 5/6 min; roughly symmetric, so mean/MAD are reasonable..

examples.q: Six students recorded reading times (minutes): 3, 8, 8, 13, 13, 18. Part A: enter the mean. Part B: enter the MAD and interpret it in minutes.
examples.steps: Mean = 63/6 = 21/2. Absolute deviations: 15/2, 5/2, 5/2, 5/2, 5/2, 15/2. Their sum divided by 6 is 25/6. This is the average distance from the mean.
worked_steps: Find the mean.
Absolute deviations: 15/2, 5/2, 5/2, 5/2, 5/2, 15/2.
Their sum divided by 6 is 25/6.
This is the average distance from the mean.

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5. Write a summary with count, attribute, units, center, variability, shape, and a justified choice of measures.
problems.a: 6 observations of reading time in minutes. Mean 7/2 min, MAD 5/6 min; roughly symmetric, so mean/MAD are reasonable.
problems.steps: Calculate the center and spread before interpreting them in context. Other accurate, justified summaries are acceptable.

problems.q: Are 5(x + 3) and 5x + 15 equivalent for every x? Use a property or a counterexample.
problems.steps: 5(x + 3) = 5x + 15. This matches.

problems.q: Which values in {9, 10, 11} satisfy x < 10? Test each by substitution.
problems.steps: Values below 10 work; the endpoint does not work.

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 7, 10, 10, 13, 13, 16. Calculate the mean and MAD. Show all absolute deviations.
Reading times in minutes are 5, 7, 7, 9, 9, 11. Write a summary with count, attribute, units, center, variability, shape, and a justified choice of measures.
problems.a: 6 observations of reading time in minutes. Mean 8 min, MAD 5/3 min; roughly symmetric, so mean/MAD are reasonable.
problems.steps: Calculate the center and spread before interpreting them in context. Other accurate, justified summaries are acceptable.

problems.q: Are 6(x + 2) and 6x + 12 equivalent for every x? Use a property or a counterexample.
problems.steps: 6(x + 2) = 6x + 12. This matches.

problems.q: Which values in {10, 11, 12} satisfy x < 11? Does the real-number inequality have only these solutions? Explain.
problems.a: 10; no, infinitely many real values satisfy it
problems.steps: Values below 11 work; the endpoint does not work.

problems.q: Six students recorded reading times (minutes): 3, 7, 7, 11, 11, 15. Part A: enter the mean. Part B: enter the MAD and interpret it in minutes.
problems.steps: Mean = 54/6 = 9. Absolute deviations: 6, 2, 2, 2, 2, 6. Their sum divided by 6 is 10/3. This is the average distance from the mean.

problems.q: Six students recorded reading times (minutes): 5, 11, 11, 17, 17, 31. Part A: describe center and spread using appropriate measures. Part B: describe shape, count, units, and any striking value; justify the chosen measures.
problems.a: 6 observations; minutes; median 14, IQR 6; mean 46/3, MAD 19/3. A high value makes median/IQR a useful choice.
problems.steps: Order the observations. Middle positions give median 14 and half medians give IQR 6. Mean is 92/6; averaging distances gives MAD 19/3. Tie the chosen summary to the displayed shape and context.

problems.q: Are 3(x + 4) and 3x + 12 equivalent for every x? Use a property or a counterexample.
problems.steps: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. This matches.

days.unit_name: AASA Applications and Cumulative Review
days.title: Course Final Test
days.target: I can apply and explain Grade 6 mathematics across the full course.

problems.q: Use the standard algorithm: 39.5 + 8.2. Show your regrouping or division steps.
problems.steps: Align decimal points; 39.5 + 8.2 = 47.7.

problems.q: Write 4^3 as repeated multiplication and evaluate.
problems.steps: The exponent counts 3 factors of 4; multiply all factors.

problems.q: A tray has 5 red tiles and 5 blue tiles. Write the red-to-blue ratio in simplest form.
problems.steps: Keep red first; divide 5:5 by 5.

problems.q: A marker is 20 m below sea level. Write its signed elevation and explain what elevation 0 means.
problems.steps: Sea level is the reference. Below is negative and above is positive.

problems.q: For 2x + 7y + 4, list terms, coefficients, and the constant.
problems.steps: Terms are separated by addition; coefficients multiply variables.

problems.q: A class studies a collection of dogs. Select all statistical questions, and identify the expected variability.
problems.a: B, D - How does mass vary among the dogs?; What is the mass in kilograms of each of the dogs?
problems.steps: Different dogs can have different mass. The questions anticipate variation across a collection. The conversion and arithmetic questions have fixed answers.

options.label: A
options.text: How many centimeters are in 4 meters?

options.label: B
options.text: How does mass vary among the dogs?

options.label: D
options.text: What is the mass in kilograms of each of the dogs?

problems.q: Use long division: 300 ÷ 5. Show the algorithm and check.
problems.steps: 30 ÷ 5: write 6, subtract 30, remainder 0; bring down the next digit: 0 ÷ 5: write 0, subtract 0, remainder 0. Check: 5 × 60 = 300.

problems.q: Solve x + 2 = 6. Check in the original equation.
problems.steps: Subtract 2 on both sides. Then x = 4; substitution gives 6 on each side.

problems.q: Use the standard algorithm: 2.6 - 1.63. Show your regrouping or division steps. Select one answer, then justify it with a model or calculation.
problems.steps: Align decimal points; 2.6 - 1.63 = 0.97.

problems.q: A recipe uses 3 cups oats for 2 cups seeds. Select all (oats, seeds) pairs that keep this ratio.
problems.steps: Equivalent ratios multiply both quantities by the same factor. A uses 2; B uses 3. C and D change only one scaled quantity.

problems.q: Evaluate 3² + 4(5 - 3). Part A: enter the value. Part B: a student begins by adding 3² and 4; explain why that changes the expression.
problems.steps: Parentheses: 5 - 3 = 2. Exponent: 3² = 9. Multiply: 4 × 2 = 8. Add: 9 + 8 = 17. The product must be completed before the final sum.

problems.q: Use the standard algorithm: 1.92 × 1.4. Show your regrouping or division steps. Select one answer, then justify it with a model or calculation.
problems.steps: Compute the whole-number product and restore decimal places: 1.92 × 1.4 = 2.688.

problems.q: A triangle has base 14 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Select all expressions that give its area in cm².
problems.steps: Triangle area is half the matching parallelogram: (14 × 5)/2 = 35 cm². Multiplying half the base by the height gives the same result.

problems.q: A student buys x markers at $5 each and y folders at $2 each, then uses one $2 coupon. Part A: enter an expression for the total cost. Part B: explain why the coupon is subtracted only once.
problems.steps: Marker cost is 5x; folder cost is 2y. Add these subtotals, then subtract the one fixed coupon of 2. An expression does not need an equals sign.

problems.q: Use the standard algorithm: 13.75 ÷ 2.5. Show your regrouping or division steps. Select one answer, then justify it with a model or calculation.
problems.steps: Multiply both numbers by 10: 137.5 ÷ 25 = 5.5. Check: 2.5 × 5.5 = 13.75.

problems.q: Draw a double number line for 3 liters of paint covering 3 m². Part A: align 0, 1, 2, and 7 batches. Part B: enter the area covered by 21 liters and explain why the scales can be different.
problems.steps: Each aligned jump adds 3 liters and 3 m². Both quantities scale by 7; the number lines measure different units.

problems.q: Let x = 3/2 and y = 3. Evaluate 7x + y². Part A: enter the value. Part B: show substitution and the order of operations.
problems.steps: Substitute: 7 × (3/2) + 3². The product is 21/2 and the square is 9. Add to get 39/2.

problems.q: Draw a bar partitioned into 4 equal parts. Shade 2 parts. Circle groups of 1 parts. Use the model to find 1/2 ÷ 1/4. Select one answer, then justify it with a model or calculation.
problems.steps: Each small part is 1/4; 2 shaded parts divided into groups of 1 gives 2/1 = 2 groups.

problems.q: 5 notebooks cost $25. Select all statements at the same price per notebook.
problems.a: C, D - 3 notebooks cost $15.; Each notebook costs $5.
problems.steps: Cost per notebook = 25 ÷ 5 = 5. Multiply $5 by the chosen notebook count.

problems.q: Select all expressions equivalent to 2(x + 4).
problems.steps: Distribute 2 to both terms to get 2x + 8. Reversing the addends gives the same value. The other expressions fail, for example at x = 0.

problems.q: Calculate 7/4 ÷ 3/5. Simplify. Select one answer, then justify it with a model or calculation.
A 10 m by 10 m rectangle has a right-triangle corner removed with perpendicular legs 4 m and 6 m. Part A: enter the removed area. Part B: enter the remaining area and justify subtraction.
problems.steps: Outer area = 100. Triangle = 4 × 6/2 = 12. Subtract the removed region exactly once.

problems.q: Select all expressions equivalent to 5x + 6x + 5.
problems.steps: Combine coefficients of like x terms: 5 + 6 = 11. The constant 5 stays separate.

problems.q: Calculate 5 ÷ 2 1/2. Simplify. Select one answer, then justify it with a model or calculation.
Store A sells 6 notebooks for $24. Store B sells 7 notebooks for $35. Part A: enter the unit price at each store. Part B: choose the better buy and explain why package totals alone are insufficient.
problems.a: A: $4 each; B: $5 each; A is the better buy.
problems.steps: Divide each cost by its own notebook count: 24/6 = 4; 35/7 = 5. Compare the same one-notebook unit.

problems.q: Select all expressions equivalent to 6(x + 4).
problems.steps: Distribute 6 to both terms to get 6x + 24. Reversing the addends gives the same value. The other expressions fail, for example at x = 0.

problems.q: Select all true statements about 12 and 18. Explain why the greatest factor fits the kit situation.
problems.a: A, D - 6 is the largest number of identical no-leftover kits from 12 pencils and 18 erasers.; 6 divides both 12 and 18.
problems.steps: GCF(12, 18) = 6. Divide each count by 6: 2 pencils and 3 erasers per kit. A larger shared divisor is impossible.

options.label: A
options.text: 6 is the largest number of identical no-leftover kits from 12 pencils and 18 erasers.

problems.q: Six students recorded reading times (minutes): 5, 8, 8, 11, 11, 14. Part A: draw a box plot and label its five-number summary. Part B: enter the IQR.
problems.steps: Minimum and maximum anchor whiskers. Box ends are 8, 11; median line is 19/2. IQR = 11 - 8.

problems.q: Solve x - 5/2 = 2. Select every representation of the solution.
problems.steps: Use the inverse operation on both sides. The solution is 9/2; the doubled numerator and denominator name the same value. Substitution verifies the solution.

problems.q: A bicycle travels 40 km in 2 hours at constant speed. Select all true statements.
problems.a: B, D - In 2 hours it travels 40 km.; The speed is 20 km per hour.
problems.steps: Divide distance by time: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 km/h. Multiply this unit rate by 2 for the later distance.

options.label: A
options.text: The speed is 42 km per hour.

options.label: D
options.text: The speed is 20 km per hour.

problems.q: Temperatures are -9 °C and -7 °C. Select all true comparisons.
problems.a: B, C - -9 < -7; -7 lies to the right of -9 on a number line.
problems.steps: Among negatives, the number closer to zero is greater. Thus -7 is warmer and is farther right.

options.label: C
options.text: -7 lies to the right of -9 on a number line.

problems.q: Solve 2 × x = 7. Select every representation of the solution.
problems.steps: Use the inverse operation on both sides. The solution is 7/2; the doubled numerator and denominator name the same value. Substitution verifies the solution.

problems.q: Use 1 feet = 12 inches. Select all statements equivalent to 7/2 feet.
problems.steps: There are 12 smaller units in each larger one. Multiply 7/2 by 12, giving 42 inches. The physical length does not change.

problems.q: Consider -9 and 7. Select all true statements.
problems.a: A, D - -9 is farther from zero than 7.; |-9| = 9
problems.steps: Absolute value measures distance: 9 versus 7. A larger distance does not make the negative number greater.

problems.q: Solve x ÷ 3 = 13/6. Select every representation of the solution.
problems.steps: Use the inverse operation on both sides. The solution is 13/2; the doubled numerator and denominator name the same value. Substitution verifies the solution.

problems.q: A school club has 80 members; 15% take part in a project. Part A: enter the number of participants. Part B: write an equation and explain whether the answer is greater or less than the whole.
problems.a: 12 participants; n = (15/100) × 80; less than the whole because the percent is below 100
problems.steps: Rename 15% as 3/20. Multiply by 80 to obtain 12. Compare the rate with 1.

problems.q: A closed box is 6 cm by 2 cm by 3 cm. Part A: enter its surface area. Part B: the 6-by-2 top is removed; enter the remaining surface area and explain.
problems.steps: Closed area = 2(12+18+6) = 72. Subtract exactly one top face, 12, for the open box.

problems.q: Reading-time frequencies (minutes) are 0–4: 3, 5–9: 4, 10–14: 5, 15–19: 4. Part A: draw a histogram. Part B: enter the observation count and name every highest-frequency interval.
problems.steps: Use four equal-width touching bars with heights 3, 4, 5, 4. Frequencies sum to 16. Include every interval with frequency 5.

problems.q: A jug contains 2 L. Each full bottle needs 4/3 L. How many full bottles can be filled, and how much liquid remains?
problems.steps: 2 ÷ 4/3 = 2 × 3/4 = 3/2. Only whole bottles count; subtract the liquid used.

problems.q: Select all values of x from the list that make x + 2 > 5 true. Explain why each rejected value fails.
problems.steps: Subtract 2 conceptually: x must exceed 3. Equality at 3 fails because the inequality is strict.

problems.q: 75 is 125% of an unknown quantity w. Select all equations that find w.
problems.steps: The part is percent rate times whole. Divide 75 by 5/4; w = 60. Check by multiplication.

problems.q: Plot P(-7, 4), Q(7, -4), and R(0, -4). Part A: name the quadrant of P and Q. Part B: explain why R is not in a quadrant.
problems.a: P: II; Q: IV; R is on the y-axis.
problems.steps: P has signs (-,+), so II. Q has (+,-), so IV. R has x = 0 and is on an axis.

problems.q: A club needs at least 4 members. Select all true statements for its membership count n.
problems.a: A, C - n ≥ 4; 4 is an allowed membership count.
problems.steps: At least includes the boundary, so n ≥ 4. On a real number line use a closed point and shade right; actual member counts are whole numbers.

problems.q: A prism measures 13/2 m by 5/2 m by 1 m. Part A: enter its volume. Part B: how many cubes with edge 1/2 m fill it? Explain why the cube count differs from the cubic-meter volume.
problems.steps: Multiply edges: 13/2 × 5/2 × 1 = 65/4. The edge counts are 13, 5, 2, giving 130 cubes. Each cube is 1/8 m³; 130/8 = 65/4.

problems.q: A quantity changes from a reference whole of 100 to a compared amount of 20. Part A: the compared amount is what percent of the reference whole? Part B: explain which number belongs in the denominator.
problems.steps: Percent = (20 ÷ 100) × 100 = 20%. The denominator is the reference whole, not automatically the larger number.

problems.q: Plot A(-2, -3), B(3, -3), and C(-2, 3). Part A: enter AB. Part B: enter AC and explain how zero helps find each distance.
problems.steps: AB is horizontal: 2 + 3 = 5. AC is vertical: 3 + 3 = 6. Each segment crosses an axis.

problems.q: A machine uses 4 liters per hour. Part A: complete the (hours, liters) table: (0, __), (1, __), (2, __). Part B: choose the independent variable and write an equation for L in terms of h. Plot your pairs.
problems.steps: Hours are the input. Multiply each hour value by 4 to obtain liters. Graph hours horizontally and liters vertically.

problems.q: Six students recorded reading times (minutes): 2, 8, 8, 14, 14, 28. Part A: describe center and spread using appropriate measures. Part B: describe shape, count, units, and any striking value; justify the chosen measures.
problems.a: 6 observations; minutes; median 11, IQR 6; mean 37/3, MAD 19/3. A high value makes median/IQR a useful choice.
problems.steps: Order the observations. Middle positions give median 11 and half medians give IQR 6. Mean is 74/6; averaging distances gives MAD 19/3. Tie the chosen summary to the displayed shape and context.

6.RP.A.1.description: Describe multiplicative ratio relationships using clear labels and ratio language.

6.RP.A.2.description: Interpret unit rates and state what the rate per one unit means.

6.RP.A.3a.description: Use tables, missing values, graphs, and comparisons of equivalent ratios.

6.RP.A.3c.description: Solve percent situations with the part, whole, or rate unknown.

6.NS.A.1.description: Interpret and compute fraction quotients with equations and visual models.

6.NS.B.2.description: Use the standard algorithm to divide multi-digit whole numbers fluently.

6.NS.B.3.description: Use standard algorithms for all four operations with decimals.

6.NS.B.4a.description: Find greatest common factors with whole numbers no greater than 100.

6.NS.B.4b.description: Find least common multiples with whole numbers no greater than 12.

6.NS.B.4c.description: Factor a sum using a common factor and the distributive property.

6.NS.C.5.description: Represent opposite real-world quantities with signs and explain zero.

6.NS.C.6a.description: Recognize opposites, double opposites, and zero as its own opposite.

6.NS.C.6b.description: Connect coordinate signs with quadrants and axis reflections.

6.NS.C.6c.description: Locate rational numbers on number lines and coordinate planes.

6.NS.C.7b.description: Explain order comparisons in real-world contexts.

6.NS.C.7c.description: Interpret absolute value as distance or magnitude.

6.NS.C.7d.description: Distinguish order comparisons from comparisons of magnitude.

6.NS.C.8.description: Graph in four quadrants and use coordinates to find aligned distances.

6.EE.A.1.description: Write and evaluate expressions with whole-number exponents.

6.EE.A.2a.description: Translate operations involving numbers and variables into expressions.

6.EE.A.2b.description: Name terms, sums, factors, products, quotients, and coefficients.

6.EE.A.2c.description: Evaluate expressions and formulas in the correct operation order.

6.EE.A.3.description: Use operation properties to generate equivalent expressions.

6.EE.A.4.description: Determine and justify whether expressions are equivalent.

6.EE.B.5.description: Use substitution to determine whether a value satisfies an equation or inequality.

6.EE.B.6.description: Define and use variables for unknown or varying numbers in context.

6.EE.B.7.description: Solve addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division one-step equations with nonnegative rational values.

6.EE.B.8.description: Write and graph strict and inclusive inequalities; recognize infinitely many solutions.

6.EE.C.9.description: Relate two changing quantities using equations, tables, and graphs.

6.G.A.1.description: Find polygon areas through composition and decomposition.

6.G.A.2.description: Connect fractional unit-cube packing with right rectangular prism volume.

6.G.A.3.description: Draw coordinate polygons and calculate horizontal and vertical side lengths.

6.G.A.4.description: Draw nets and use face areas to calculate surface area.

6.SP.A.1.description: Recognize questions that anticipate variability in collected data.

6.SP.A.2.description: Describe distributions by center, spread, and overall shape.

6.SP.A.3.description: Distinguish measures of center from measures of variability.

6.SP.B.4.description: Construct and interpret dot plots, histograms, and box plots.

6.SP.B.5b.description: Name the investigated attribute, measurement method, and units.

6.SP.B.5c.description: Summarize center and variability and explain patterns or unusual values in context.

6.SP.B.5d.description: Choose center and variability measures suited to the distribution and context.
